chapters.title: Introduction: Science as Agreement & The Categorical Pipeline
chapters.theme: Why informal diagrams fail without functional semantics; science as interpersonal and experimental agreement; category theory as a formal bridge across scientific disciplines.
global_invariants: Every arrow in a rigorous model must represent a well-defined morphism (function) in an explicit context.

Hierarchies are partial orders, symmetries are group elements, data models are categories, agent actions are monoid actions, local-to-global principles are sheaves, self-similarity is modeled by operads, and context is modeled by monads (p. 14).

chapters.title: The Category of Sets, Commutative Diagrams, and Ologs
chapters.theme: Grounding mathematical modeling in Set: sets, functions, isomorphisms, commutative diagrams, and Ontology Logs (ologs) as functional worldviews.
global_invariants: Two paths in a diagram commute iff their composite functions are equal on every input element.
An olog is a rigorous worldview schema whose boxes are types (sets), arrows are functional aspects, and commuting paths are declared facts.

chapters.title: Fundamental Considerations in Set: Limits, Colimits & Universal Constructions
chapters.theme: Universal constructions in Set: products, coproducts, pullbacks (fiber products), spans, equalizers, equivalence relations, pushouts, currying (exponentials), and subobject classifiers.
global_invariants: Limits in Set (products, pullbacks, equalizers, terminal object) carve out constrained subsets of tuples satisfying equations.
Colimits in Set (coproducts, pushouts, coequalizers, initial object) glue sets together by quotienting disjoint unions along shared overlaps.

chapters.title: Categories and Functors, Without Admitting It: Monoids, Groups, Graphs, Orders & Databases
chapters.theme: Concrete scientific modeling structures before abstracting to general categories: monoids (agent actions/FSMs), groups (symmetries), graphs (paths), orders (hierarchies/topologies), and categorical databases (schemas + instances).
global_invariants: A database schema (G, ~) is a directed graph equipped with a congruence (path equivalence relation) on paths.
A database instance on schema C assigns a set of rows to each table (vertex) and a foreign-key function to each arrow respecting path equivalences.

chapters.title: Basic Category Theory: Categories, Functors, Natural Transformations & Cat ≃ Sch
chapters.theme: The core triad of category theory—categories, functors, and natural transformations—culminating in the equivalence of categories and database schemas (Cat ≃ Sch).
global_invariants: Monoids are 1-object categories; groups are 1-object categories with invertible morphisms; preorders are categories with at most one morphism between any two objects.
Database schemas and small categories are categorically equivalent (Cat ≃ Sch), and database instances are Set-valued functors I : C -> Set.

chapters.title: Fundamental Considerations of Categories: Universal Limits, Colimits & Grothendieck Construction
chapters.theme: Lifting limits and colimits to arbitrary categories via universal cones/cocones, opposite categories (duality), the Grothendieck construction (category of elements), and comma/slice categories.
global_invariants: Every colimit in C is a limit in C^op; universal properties determine objects uniquely up to unique isomorphism.
The Grothendieck construction integral(I) converts a Set-valued functor (database instance or presheaf) into a discrete opfibration over its base schema C.

chapters.title: Categories at Work: Adjoint Functors, Data Migration, Sheaves, Monads & Operads
chapters.theme: High-power categorical machinery for scientific synthesis: adjunctions (L -| R), Kan data migration (Sigma_F -| Delta_F -| Pi_F), presheaves, Yoneda's lemma, sheaves (local-to-global gluing of worldviews), monads (context), and operads (hierarchical self-similarity).
global_invariants: Given a schema functor F : C -> D, pullback data migration Delta_F has both a left adjoint Sigma_F (disjoint union / Skolemization) and a right adjoint Pi_F (fibered product / join).
A presheaf O : Open(X)^op -> Set (or Sch) is a sheaf iff compatible local sections on any open cover {V_i} glue uniquely into a global section on U = union(V_i).

stalks.title: Science as Agreement & Categorical Worldviews
stalks.summary: Science is the pursuit of rigorous agreement—between observation and hypothesis, and between communicating minds. Informal boxes-and-arrows (like Figure 1.1) create an illusion of agreement unless grounded in functions, data, and explicit context.
stalks.formal_core: A scientific worldview is formalized as a category C (or schema/olog) together with an instance functor I : C -> Set (empirical data). Interpersonal communication is a functor F : C_1 -> C_2; shared understanding on an overlap is a sheaf gluing condition.

stalks.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
stalks.summary: The foundational category Set whose objects are sets (collections of distinct elements) and whose morphisms are functions f : X -> Y assigning to each x in X a unique f(x) in Y, equipped with associative composition and identity functions.
stalks.formal_core: Ob(Set) = sets; Hom_Set(X, Y) = {f : X -> Y}. Composition (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)) satisfies (h o g) o f = h o (g o f) and id_Y o f = f = f o id_X. A function f : X -> Y is an isomorphism (X ~= Y) iff there exists g : Y -> X with g o f = id_X and f o g = id_Y.

an element z of target Z

aspects.label: maps via composite g ∘ f to

facts: Path equivalence: for every x in X, applying f then g yields (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)).
Isomorphism (Def 2.1.2.14, p. 38): f : X -> Y has inverse g : Y -> X iff f is both injective and surjective (bijective).

formal_items.title: Isomorphism
formal_items.text: Definition 2.1.2.14 (Isomorphism). Let X and Y be sets. A function f : X → Y is called an isomorphism, denoted f : X→≅Y, if there exists a function g : Y → X such that g ○ f = idX and f ○ g = idY. Figure 2.4 An isomorphism X→≅Y.

formal_items.title: Cardinality of finite sets
formal_items.text: Definition 2.1.2.23 (Cardinality of finite sets). Let A be a set and n ∈ ℕ a natural number. We say that A has cardinality n, denoted |A|=n, if there exists an isomorphism of sets A ≅ n. If there exists some n ∈ ℕ such that A has cardinality n, then we say that A is finite. Otherwise, we say that A is infinite and write |A| ∞.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Proposition 2.1.2.18. The following facts hold about isomorphism. 1. Any set A is isomorphic to itself; i.e., there exists an isomorphism A→≅A. 2. For any sets A and B, if A is isomorphic to B, then B is isomorphic to A.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Proposition 2.1.2.25. Let A and B be finite sets. If there is an isomorphism of sets f : A → B, then the two sets have the same cardinality, |A| = |B|. Proof. If f : A → B is an isomorphism and B ≅ n, then A ≅ n because the composition of two isomorphisms is an isomorphism.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Slogan 2.1.2.1. Given a function f : X → Y, we think of X as a set of things, and Y as a set of bins. The function tells us in which bin to put each thing.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Slogan 2.1.2.7. Given composable functions X→fY→gZ, we have a way of putting every thing in X into a bin in Y, and we have a way of putting each bin from Y into a larger bin in Z. The composite, g ○ f : X → Z, is the resulting way that every thing in X is put into a bin in Z.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Application 2.1.2.2. In studying the mechanics of materials, one wishes to know how a material responds to tension. For example, a rubber band responds to tension differently than a spring does. To each material we can associate a force- extension curve, recording how much force the material carries when extended to various lengths. Once we fix a methodology for performing experiments, finding a material’s force-extension curve would ideally constitute a function from the set of materials to the set of curves.

formal_items.title: The Category Set: Sets, Functions & Isomorphisms
formal_items.text: Application 2.1.2.16. There is an isomorphism between the set NucDNA of nucleotides found in DNA and the set NucRNA of nucleotides found in RNA. Indeed, both sets have four elements, so there are 24 different isomorphisms. But only one is useful in biology. Before we say which one it is, let us say there is also an isomorphism NucDNA ≅ {A, C, G, T} and an isomorphism NucRNA ≅ {A, C, G, U}, and we will use the letters as abbreviations for the nucleotides. The convenient isomorphism NucDNA→≅NucRNA is that given by RNA transcription; it sends A↦U, C↦G, G↦C, T↦A. (See also

Protein production can be modeled as a function from the set of 3-nucleotide sequences to the set of eukaryotic amino acids. However, it cannot be an isomorphism because there are 43 = 64 triplets of RNA nucleotides but only 21 eukaryotic amino acids.

formal_items.text: Example 2.1.2.4. Suppose that X is a set and X′ ⊆ X is a subset. Then we can consider the function X′ → X given by sending every element of X′ to “itself” as an element of X. For example, if X = {a, b, c, d, e, f} and X′ = {b, d, e}, then X′ ⊆ X. We turn that into the function X′ → X given by b ↦ b, d ↦ d, e ↦ e.2 As a matter of notation, we may sometimes say the following: Let X be a set, and let i : X′ ⊆ X be a subset. Here we are making clear that X′ is a subset of X, but that i is the name of the associated function.

stalks.title: Commutative Diagrams & Path Equations
stalks.summary: Diagrams of objects and morphisms where any two directed paths with the same start and end object compose to the exact same morphism. Commutativity is the categorical replacement for algebraic equations.
stalks.formal_core: A diagram D : J -> C commutes if for every pair of parallel paths p, q : x ->* y in J, the induced composite morphisms in C satisfy D(p) = D(q). In Set, a square g o f = k o h commutes iff g(f(x)) = k(h(x)) for all x.

stalks.title: Ologs (Ontology Logs): Functional Worldviews
stalks.summary: Spivak's signature knowledge-representation formalism: an Ontology Log (olog) is a readable, mathematically rigorous category presentation where boxes are noun-phrase Types, arrows are verb-phrase Functional Aspects, and commuting diagrams are Facts.
stalks.formal_core: An olog O is a database schema (presentation of a category) with human-readable English labels obeying strict rules: (1) every Type box begins with 'a/an' representing a set of instances; (2) every Aspect arrow x --f--> y reads '[x] [f] [y]' and must be a valid mathematical function (deterministic & total); (3) Facts are declared path equivalences p ~ q.

formal_items.text: Warning 2.3.2.2. The author of an olog has a worldview, some fragment of which is captured in the olog. When person A examines the olog of person B, person A may or may not agree with it. For example, person B may have the following olog which associates to each marriage a man and a woman. Person A may take the position that some marriages involve two men or two women and thus see B’s olog as wrong. Such disputes are not “problems” with either A’s olog or B’s olog; they are discrepancies between worldviews. stalks.title: Products & Universal Pairing in Set

formal_items.text: Example 3.1.1.7. Let ℝ be the set of real numbers. By ℝ2 we mean ℝ × ℝ. Similarly, for any n ∈ ℕ, we define ℝn to be the product of n copies of ℝ. According to Penrose [35], Aristotle seems to have conceived of space as something like S ≔ ℝ3 and of time as something like T ≔ ℝ. Space-time, had he conceived of it, would probably have been S × T ≅ ℝ4. He, of course, did not have access to this kind of abstraction, which was probably due to Descartes. (The product X × Y is often called Cartesian product, in his honor.)

formal_items.title: Grid of dots, continued
formal_items.text: Example 3.1.1.11 (Grid of dots, continued). It is important that the reader sees the universal property for products as completely intuitive. Recall that if X and Y are sets, say, of cardinalities |X| = m and |Y | = n respectively, then X × Y is an m × n grid of dots, and it comes with two canonical projections X←π1X×Y→π2Y. These allow us to extract from every grid element z ∈ X × Y its column π1(z) ∈ X and its row π2(z) ∈ Y. Suppose that each person in a classroom picks an element of X and an element of Y. formal_items.text: Example 3.1.1.17. Every car owner owns at least one car, but there is no obvious function ⌜a car owner⌝ → ⌜a car⌝ because he or she may own more than one. One good choice would be the car that the person drives most often, which can be called his or her primary car. Also, given a person and a car, an economist could ask how much utility the person would get out of the car. From all this we can put together the following olog involving products: The composite map O → V tells us the utility a car owner gets out of their primary car.

formal_items.text: Remark 3.1.1.6. It is possible to take the product of more than two sets as well. For example, if A, B, and C are sets, then A × B × C is the set of triples A×B×C≔{ (a,b,c)|a∈A,b∈B,c∈C }. This kind of generality is useful in understanding multiple dimensions, e.g., what physicists mean by ten-dimensional space. It comes under the heading of limits (see Section 6.1.3).

formal_items.text: Definition 3.3.1.1 (Equivalence relations and equivalence classes). Let X be a set, and consider the product X × X, as in Definition 3.1.1.1. An equivalence relation on X is a subset R ⊆ X × X satisfying the following properties for all x, y, z ∈ X: Reflexivity: (x, x) ∈ R; Symmetry: (x, y) ∈ R if and only if (y, x) ∈ R; Transitivity: If (x, y) ∈ R and (y, z) ∈ R, then (x, z) ∈ R. If R is an equivalence relation, we often write x ∼R y, or simply x ∼ y, to mean (x, y) ∈ R. formal_items.title: Generating equivalence relations
formal_items.text: Proposition 3.3.1.7 (Generating equivalence relations). Let X be a set and R ⊆ X × X any subset. There exists a relation S ⊆ X × X such that S is an equivalence relation; R ⊆ S; for any equivalence relation S′ such that R ⊆ S′, we have S ⊆ S′. The relation S′ is called the equivalence relation generated by R. Proof. Let LR be the set of all equivalence relations on X that contain R. In other words, each element ℓ ∈ LR is an equivalence relation, so we have R ⊆ ℓ ⊆ X × X. The set LR is nonempty because X × X ⊆ X × X is an equivalence relation containing R. formal_items.text: Proposition 3.3.1.7 has the benefit of working even if |X| ∞, but it has the cost that it is not very intuitive nor useful in practice when X is finite. The intuitive way to think about the idea of equivalence relation generated by R is as follows: 1. First add to R what is demanded by reflexivity, R1 ≔ R ∪ {(x, x) | x ∈ X}. 2. To the result, add what is demanded by symmetry, R2 ≔ R1 ∪{(x, y) | (y, x) ∈ R1}. 3. Finally, to the result, add what is demanded by transitivity, S=R2∪{(x,z)|(x,y)∈R2,and (y,z)∈R2}. Then S is an equivalence relation, the smallest one containing R.

formal_items.text: Example 3.3.1.2. Let ℤ denote the set of integers. Define a relation R ⊆ ℤ × ℤ by R={(x,y)|∃n∈ℤ such that x+7n=y}. Then R is an equivalence relation because x + 7 * 0 = x (reflexivity); x + 7 * n = y if and only if y + 7 * (−n) = x (symmetry); and x + 7n = y and y + 7m = z together imply that x + 7(m + n) = z (transitivity). An example equivalence class A ⊆ ℤ for this relation is A = {…, −12, −5, 2, 9, …}.

formal_items.title: Partitions
formal_items.text: Example 3.3.1.4 (Partitions). An equivalence relation on a set X can be thought of as a way of partitioning X. A partition of X consists of a set I, called the set of parts, and for every element i ∈ I, the selection of a subset Xi ⊆ X such that two properties hold: Every element x ∈ X is in some part (i.e., for all x ∈ X, there exists i ∈ I such that x ∈ Xi). No element can be found in two different parts (i.e., if x ∈ Xi and x ∈ Xj, then i = j). We can form X ⊔ Y, but it has two copies of 1. This is weird, so we use pushouts; let W = {1}. formal_items.text: Definition 3.4.4.12 (Characteristic function). Given a subset A ⊆ X, we define its characteristic function of A in X to be the function ψ(A): X → Ω, from (3.25). formal_items.text: Definition 3.4.5.1. Let f : X → Y be a function. We say that f is injective if for all x, x′ ∈ X with f(x) = f(x′), we have x = x′. We say that f is surjective if for all y ∈ Y, there exists some x ∈ X such that f(x) = y. We say that f is bijective if it is both injective and surjective. We sometimes denote an injective function X ↪ Y, a surjective function X ↠ Y, and a bijective function X →≅ Y (see Proposition 3.4.5.4).

formal_items.title: Monomorphisms, epimorphisms
formal_items.text: Definition 3.4.5.7 (Monomorphisms, epimorphisms). Let f : X → Y be a function. We say that f is a monomorphism if for all sets A and pairs of functions g, g′ : A → X, if f ○ g = f ○ g′, then g = g′. We say that f is an epimorphism if for all sets B and pairs of functions h, h′ : Y → B, if h ○ f = h′ ○ f, then h = h′.

If m n, then there is an inclusion {1, 2, …, m} → {1, 2, …, n}. Suppose now that we are given an injection f : m → n; we assume that m > n and derive a contradiction. If m > n, then n + 1 m, and we have already shown that there exists an injection g : n + 1 ↪ m. Composing, we have an injection h ≔ g ○ f : n + 1 ↪ n by Exercise 3.4.5.3. formal_items.title: Monoid
formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.1 (Monoid). A monoid is a sequence (M, e, ⋆), where M is a set, e ∈ M is an element, and ⋆: M × M → M is a function, such that the following monoid laws hold for all m, n, p ∈ M: m ⋆ e = m. e ⋆ m = m. (m ⋆ n) ⋆ p = m ⋆ (n ⋆ p). We refer to e as the unit element and to ⋆ as the multiplication formula for the monoid.1 We call the first two rules unit laws and the third rule the associativity law for monoids.

formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.13. Let X be a set. A list in X is a pair (n, f), where n ∈ ℕ is a natural number (called the length of the list) and f : n → X is a function, where n = {1, 2, …, n}. We may denote such a list (n,f)=[f(1),f(2),…,f(n)]. The set of lists in X is denoted List(X). The empty list is the unique list in which n = 0; we may denote it [ ]. Given an element x ∈ X, the singleton list on x is the list [x]. Given a list L = (n, f) and a number i ∈ ℕ with i n, the ith entry of L is the element f(i) ∈ X. Given two lists L = (n, f) and L′ = (n′, f′), define the concatenation of L and L

formal_items.title: Monoids, Agent Actions & Finite State Machines
formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.15. Let X be a set. The free monoid generated by X is the sequence FX ≔ (List(X), [ ], ++), where List(X) is the set of lists of elements in X, [ ] ∈ List(X) is the empty list, and ++ is the operation of list concatenation. We refer to X as the set of generators for the monoid FX.

formal_items.title: Monoids, Agent Actions & Finite State Machines
formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.17. Let M≔(M,e,⋆) be a monoid. A congruence on M is an equivalence relation ∼ on M, such that for any m, m′ ∈ M and any n, n′ ∈ M, if m ∼ m′ and n ∼ n′, then m ⋆ n ∼ m′ ∼ n′.

formal_items.title: Presented monoid
formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.19 (Presented monoid). Let G be a finite set, and let R ⊆ List(G) × List(G) be a relation. The monoid presented by generators G and relations R is the monoid M = (M, e, ⋆), defined as follows. Begin with the free monoid FG = (List(G), [ ], ++) generated by G. Let ∼ denote the congruence on FG generated by R, as in Proposition 4.1.1.18, and define M ≔ FG/∼. Each element r ∈ R is of the form r = (ℓ, ℓ′) for lists ℓ, ℓ′ ∈ List(G). For historical reasons we call the each of the resulting expressions ℓ ∼ ℓ′ a relation in R.

formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.25. A monoid is called cyclic if it has a presentation involving only one generator.

formal_items.title: Monoid action

formal_items.text: Proposition 4.1.4.5. Let M=(ℤ,0,+) and M′=(ℕ,0,+) . The only monoid homomorphism f:M→M′ is trivial, i.e., it sends every element m ∈ ℤ to 0 ∈ ℕ. Proof. Let f:M→M′ be a monoid homomorphism, and let n = f(1) and n′ = f(−1) in ℕ. Then we know that since 0 = 1+(−1) in ℤ, we must have 0 = f(0) = f(1+(−1)) = f(1)+f(−1) = n+n′ ∈ ℕ. But if n 1, then this is impossible, so n = 0. Similarly, n ′ = 0. Any element m ∈ ℤ can be written as m = 1 + 1 + ⋯ + 1 or as m = −1 + −1 + ⋯ + −1, and it is easy to see that f(1) + f(1) + ⋯ + f(1) = 0 = f(−1) + f(−1) + ⋯ + f(−1). Therefore, f(m) = 0 for all m ∈ ℤ.

We have Δf(α)(e, s) = α(f(e), s) = α(e′, s) = s. We also have Δf(α)(m,Δf(α)(n,s))=α(f(m),α(f(n),s))=α(f(m)⋆′f(n),s)=α(f(m⋆n),s)=Δf(α) (m⋆n,s). Then the unit law and the multiplication law hold.

formal_items.text: Slogan 4.1.0.14. The performance of a sequence of several actions is itself the performance of an action—a more complex action, but an action nonetheless. Mathematical objects called monoids and groups are tasked with encoding the agent’s perspective, i.e., what the agent can do, and what happens when she does a sequence of actions in succession. A monoid can be construed as a set of actions together with a formula that encodes how a sequence of actions is itself considered an action. A group is the same as a monoid except that every action is required to be reversible.

stalks.title: Preorders, Partial Orders, Meets/Joins & Alexandrov Spaces
stalks.summary: Orders formalize hierarchies, taxonomies, causal structure, and open-set lattices Open(X). A preorder (P, <=) is a reflexive, transitive relation—equivalent to a category with at most one morphism between any two objects. Meets (greatest lower bounds) are categorical products; joins (least upper bounds) are categorical coproducts.
stalks.formal_core: Preorder: x <= x (reflexive) and x <= y & y <= z => x <= z (transitive) (Def 4.4.1.1, p. 223). Partial order adds antisymmetry (x <= y & y <= x => x = y). Monotone map f : P -> Q satisfies x <= y => f(x) <= f(y) (functor between thin categories). Open(X) of a topological space is a partial order under subset inclusion U <= V.

types.label: an open subregion U in Open(X)

their union cover U ∨ V = U ∪ V

facts: In a poset category (P, ≤), categorical product is Meet (x ∧ y) and categorical coproduct is Join (x ∨ y) (Sec 4.4.2, p. 231).
The opposite order P^op reverses ≤, turning inclusions U ⊆ V into restriction morphisms V -> U for presheaves Open(X)^op -> Set.

formal_items.title: Preorders, Partial Orders, Meets/Joins & Alexandrov Spaces
formal_items.text: Definition 4.4.1.1. Let S be a set and R ⊆ S × S a binary relation on S; if (s, s′) ∈ R, we write s s′. Then we say that R is a preorder if, for all s, s′, s″ ∈ S, we have Reflexivity: s s, and Transitivity: if s s′ and s′ s″, then s s″. We say that R is a partial order if it is a preorder and, in addition, for all s, s′ ∈ S, we have Antisymmetry: If s s′ and s′ s, then s = s′. We say that R is a linear order if it is a partial order and, in addition, for all s, s′ ∈ S, we have Comparability: Either s s′ or s′ s. We denote such a preorder (or partial order or linear order) by (S, ).

formal_items.text: Example 4.4.5.8. Let U = {(x, y) ∈ ℝ2 | x > 0}. To see that U is open, define the following sets: for any a, b ∈ ℝ, let S(a, b) be the square parallel to the axes, with side length 1, where the upper left corner is (a, b). Note that S(a, b) is a closed curve, so if we let S′(a, b) be the interior of S(a, b), then each S′(a, b) is a basic open set. Now U is the union of S′(a, b) over the collection of all a > 0 and all b, U=∪a,b∈ℝ,a>0 S′(a,b), so U is open.

The composition formula ○ is given by function composition, and for every set X, the identity function idX: X → X serves as the identity morphism for X ∈ Ob(Set). Every object of Fin is an object of Set, but not vice versa. Although Fin and Set have different collections of objects, their notions of morphism are in some sense the same. formal_items.text: Example 5.1.1.10 (Noncategory 2). In this example, we make a faux category F with one object and many morphisms. The problem here is the composition formula. Define F to have one object Ob(F)={☺}, and HomF(☺,☺)=ℕ . Define id ☺= 1 ∈ ℕ. Define the composition formula ○: ℕ × ℕ → ℕ by the usual exponentiation function for natural numbers, m ○ n = mn. This is a perfectly cromulent function, but it does not work right as a composition formula. Indeed, for the identity law to hold, we would need m1 = m = 1m, and one side of this is false. For the associativity law to hold, we would need (mn)p=m(np), but this is also not the case.

formal_items.text: Example 5.3.1.15. Recall that to any graph G we can associate the paths-graph Paths(G) (see Example 5.1.2.25). This is a functor Paths: Grph → Grph. There is also an identity functor idGrph : Grph → Grph. A natural transformation η : idGrph → Paths would consist of a graph homomorphism ηG : idGrph(G) → Paths(G) for every graph G. But idGrph(G) = G by definition, so we need ηG : G → Paths(G). Recall that Paths(G) has the same vertices as G, and every arrow in G counts as a path (of length 1). So there is an obvious graph homomorphism from G to Paths(G). It is not hard to see that the necessary naturality squares commute.

formal_items.text: Proposition 6.1.3.15. Let C be a category, and let a1,a2∈Ob(C) both be initial objects. Then there is a unique isomorphism f:a1→≅a2. (Similarly, for any two terminal objects in C, there is a unique isomorphism between them.) Proof. Suppose a1 and a2 are initial. Since a1 is initial, there is a unique morphism f : a1 → a2; there is also a unique morphism a1 → a1, which must be ida1. Since a2 is initial, there is a unique morphism g : a2 → a1; there is also a unique morphism a2 → a2, which must be ida2. So g ○ f = ida1 and f ○ g = ida2, which means that f is the desired (unique) isomorphism.

An element of the set colimI F is given by choosing any i ∈ Ob(I) and any element of xi ∈ F(i), and then considering two such elements equivalent if there exists f : i → i′ such that X(f)(xi) = xi′. Proof. See [29].

stalks.title: Opposite Categories, Grothendieck Construction ∫I & Comma Categories
stalks.summary: Three structural operations on categories: (1) Opposite category C^op reverses all arrows (turning presheaves C^op -> Set into covariant functors); (2) The Grothendieck construction (category of elements ∫I) flattens a Set-valued functor I : C -> Set into a single category fibred over C (turning a database instance into anRDF-like typed graph with projection pi : ∫I -> C); (3) Slice (C/x) and Comma categories ((F ↓ G)) localize morphisms over a base context.
stalks.formal_core: Grothendieck Construction (Def 6.2.2.1, p. 444): Given I : C -> Set, the category of elements integral(I) has objects (c, x) with c in Ob(C) and x in I(c), and morphisms f : (c, x) -> (c', x') given by f : c -> c' in C such that I(f)(x) = x', equipped with a faithful projection functor pi : integral(I) -> C.

formal_items.title: Opposite Categories, Grothendieck Construction ∫I & Comma Categories
formal_items.text: Definition 6.2.2.1. Let C be a category, and let J:C→Set be a functor. The category of elements of J, denoted ∫CJ, is defined as follows: Ob(∫CJ)≔{(C,x)|C∈Ob(C),x∈J(C)};Hom∫CJ((C,x),(C′,x′))≔{f:C→C ′|J(f)(x)=x′}. There is a natural functor πJ:∫CJ→C. It sends each object (C,x)∈Ob(∫CJ) to the object C∈Ob(C). And it sends each morphism f : (C, x) → (C′, x′) to the morphism f : C → C′. We call πJ the projection functor.

stalks.title: Adjoint Functors (L ⊣ R) & Universal Dictionary Bridges
stalks.summary: When two categories C and D have different levels of structure (e.g., Sets vs. Monoids, Graphs vs. Categories, Preorders vs. Topological Spaces), an adjunction L : C <-> D : R provides the optimal two-way translation dictionary. Left adjoints L are 'liberal/free' and preserve colimits (LAPC); right adjoints R are 'conservative/constrained' and preserve limits (RAPL).
stalks.formal_core: Definition 7.1.1.2 (p. 467): L : C -> D is left adjoint to R : D -> C (written L -| R) if there is a bijection alpha_{c,d} : Hom_D(L(c), d) ~= Hom_C(c, R(d)) natural in both c in C and d in D. Equivalently characterized by unit eta : id_C => R o L and counit epsilon : L o R => id_D satisfying the triangle identities. Proposition 7.1.3.1 (p. 478): Right adjoints preserve limits (RAPL); left adjoints preserve colimits (LAPC).

formal_items.text: Proposition 7.1.3.1. Let L:B⇄A :R be an adjunction. For any indexing category I and functor D : I → B, if D has a colimit in B, then there is a unique isomorphism L(colim D)≅colim(L○D). Similarly, for any I ∈ Ob(Cat) and functor D:I→A, if D has a limit in A, then there is a unique isomorphism R(limD)≅lim(R○D). Proof. formal_items.text: Example 7.1.1.5. Let L: Set → Mon and R: Mon → Set be the free and forgetful functors from Proposition 7.1.1.2. We know that L is left adjoint to R; however L is not right adjoint to R. In other words, we can show that the necessary natural isomorphism cannot exist. Let X = {a, b}, and let M = 1 be the trivial monoid. Then the necessary natural isomorphism would need to give a bijection HomMon(M,L(X))≅?HomSet({1},X). But the left-hand side has one element, because M is the initial object in Mon (see Example 6.1.3.7), whereas the right-hand side has two elements. Therefore, no isomorphism can exist.

formal_items.text: Example 7.1.1.6. Preorders have underlying sets, giving rise to a functor U : PrO → Set. The functor U has both a left adjoint and a right adjoint. The left adjoint of U is D : Set → PrO, sending a set X to the discrete preorder on X (the preorder with underlying set X, having the fewest possible ’s). The right adjoint of U is I : Set → PrO, sending a set X to the indiscrete preorder on X (the preorder with underlying set X, having the most possible ’s). See Example 4.4.4.5.

This means that L preserves colimits. So taking the union of graphs G and H results in a graph whose path poset L(G ⊔ H) is the union of the path posets of G and H. formal_items.text: Definition 7.2.1.4 (Monomorphism, epimorphism). Let S be a category, and let f : X → Y be a morphism. We say that f is a monomorphism if it has the following property. For all objects A∈Ob(S) and morphisms g, g′ : A → X in S, if f ○ g = f ○ g′, then g = g′. We say that f : X → Y is an epimorphism if it has the following property. For all objects B∈Ob(S) and morphisms h, h′ : Y → B in S, if h ○ f = h′ ○ f, then h = h′. In the category of sets, monomorphisms are the same as injections, and epimorphisms are the same as surjections (see Proposition 3.4.5.8). formal_items.text: Proposition 7.2.1.15 (Yoneda’s lemma, part 1). Let C be a category, c∈Ob(C) an object, and I:C→Set a set-valued functor. There is a natural bijection HomC−Set(Yc,I)→≅I(c). Proof. See Mac Lane [29].

stalks.summary: A presheaf O : Open(X)^op -> Set assigns to each open region U <= X a set O(U) of valid local sections ('value assignments throughout U') and to each inclusion U' <= U a restriction map rho_{U',U} : O(U) -> O(U') (written a |-> a|_{U'}). A presheaf is a SHEAF if for every open cover U = union_i V_i, any family of local sections a_i in O(V_i) that agree on all pairwise overlaps (a_i|_{V_i n V_j} = a_j|_{V_i n V_j}) glues uniquely into a single global section b in O(U) with b|_{V_i} = a_i.

Equivalently, O(U) -> prod_i O(V_i) ==> prod_{i,j} O(V_i n V_j) is an equalizer diagram in Set.

stalks.title: Sheaf of Ologged Concepts, Alexandrov Sites & Descent Data
stalks.summary: The theoretical heart of our Sheaf Knowledge Base (Section 7.2.3.11, p. 523–524): Spivak upgrades sheaves of sets to a SHEAF OF OLOGGED CONCEPTS (a sheaf of categories/schemas O : Open(X)^op -> Sch). Given a simplicial complex X of agents or conceptual domains, each vertex v holds a local worldview olog O(v), and each higher simplex u holds the common-ground olog O(u) with restriction schema morphisms O(v) -> O(u). Applying the Alexandrov functor Alx(X^op) yields a topological space whose sheaf of categories glues local ologs into a globally consistent worldview!
stalks.formal_core: Section 7.2.3.11 (p. 523–524): Given a simplicial complex X (a sub-poset of P(X_0) ordered by inclusion u <= v), assign to each simplex a schema/olog via a functor O : X -> Sch, where u <= v induces a restriction map of ologs O(v) -> O(u) ('any idea shared among all vertices in v is shared among the subset u'). Under the Alexandrov functor Alx : PrO -> Top on X^op, O extends uniquely to a sheaf of categories/schemas on X = Alx(X^op). Remark 7.2.3.6 (p. 521): When local sensors/experts use different vocabularies on overlaps U_{i,j}, they glue via isomorphic Descent Data p_{i,j} : T_i|_{U_{i,j}} ->~ T_j|_{U_{i,j}} satisfying the cocycle condition.

stalks.title: Monads (T, η, μ): Formalizing Experimental & Computational Context
stalks.symbol: (T : C → C, η : id ⇒ T, μ : T∘T ⇒ T)
stalks.summary: In pure Set, functions must be total, deterministic, and context-free. In real science and computing, processes may fail (partiality B ⊔ {☺}), produce multiple outcomes (powerset P(B)), carry probabilistic uncertainty (Dist(B)), or depend on an experimental environment (B^E). A monad (T, eta, mu) packages such a context functor T with a unit natural transformation eta (injecting a pure value into a trivial context) and a multiplication natural transformation mu (flattening nested contexts T(T(B)) -> T(B)).
stalks.formal_core: Definition 7.3.2.1 (p. 533): A monad on C consists of an endofunctor T : C -> C, a unit natural transformation eta : id_C => T, and a multiplication natural transformation mu : T o T => T obeying: (1) Left/Right Unit Laws: mu o (T eta) = id_T = mu o (eta T); (2) Associativity Law: mu o (T mu) = mu o (mu T).

formal_items.text: Example 7.3.2.4 (Partial functions as a monad). Here is the monad for partial functions, as discussed in Example 7.3.1.1. The functor T : Set → Set sends a set X to the set X ⊔ {☺}. Clearly, given a function f : X → Y, there is an induced function (f ⊔ {☺}) : (X ⊔ {☺}) → (Y ⊔ {☺}), so this is a functor. The natural transformation η : id → T is given on a set X by the component function ηX:X→X⊔{☺} that includes X ↪ X ⊔ {☺}. Finally, the natural transformation µ : T ○ T → T is given on a set X by the component function µX:X⊔{☺}⊔{☺}→X⊔{☺} that collapses both copies of ☺.

stalks.title: Operads, Wiring Diagrams & Hierarchical Self-Similarity
stalks.summary: While a category only allows 1-to-1 morphisms f : x -> y, an operad O generalizes categories to multi-input morphisms f : (x_1, ..., x_n) -> y that can be recursively nested inside one another like hierarchical wiring diagrams, fractal squares (Little Cubes operad), or multi-scale biological materials (collagen fibrils -> fibers -> tendon). An operad algebra F : O -> Set populates each box with a set of possible states and each wiring diagram with a composition operation combining part states into whole-system states.
stalks.formal_core: Definition 7.4.1.1 (p. 559): An operad O specifies objects Ob(O), multi-hom sets O_n(x_1,...,x_n; y), identity morphisms id_x in O_1(x; x), and substitution/composition maps O_n(y_1,...,y_n; z) × prod_i O_{k_i}(x_{i,1},...,x_{i,k_i}; y_i) -> O_{sum k_i}(x...; z) obeying identity and associativity laws. Operad algebra (Def 7.4.2.1, p. 567): A functor of operads A : O -> Set.

formal_items.title: Operads, Wiring Diagrams & Hierarchical Self-Similarity
formal_items.text: Definition 7.4.1.1. An operad O is defined as follows: One announces some constituents (A. objects, B. morphisms, C. identities, D. compositions) and shows that they conform to some laws (1. identity law, 2. associativity law). Specifically, one announces A. a collection Ob(O), each element of which is called an object of O; B. for each object y∈Ob(O), finite set n ∈ Ob(Fin), and n-indexed set of objects x:n→Ob(O), a set On(x;y)∈Ob(Set); its elements are called morphisms from x to y in O; C. for every object x∈Ob(O), a specified morphism, denoted idx∈O1(x;x) and called the identity morphism on x.

formal_items.text: Definition 7.4.1.8. Let O and O′ be operads. An operad functor from O to O′, denoted F:O→O′, is defined as follows. One announces some constituents (A. on-objects part, B. on-morphisms part) and shows that they conform to some laws (1. preservation of identities, 2. preservation of composition). Specifically, one announces A. a function Ob(F):Ob(O)→Ob(O′), sometimes denoted simply F:Ob(O)→Ob(O′); B. for each object y∈Ob(O), finite set n ∈ Ob(Fin), and n-indexed set of objects x:n→Ob(O), a function Fn:On(x;y)→On′(Fx;Fy). two_simplices.title: The Schema-Category-Instance Gluing Triangle

two_simplices.law: Restricting a sheaf O : Open(X)^op -> Set to a binary cover {U, V} exhibits O(U ∪ V) as the fiber product O(U) ×_{O(U ∩ V)} O(V).

two_simplices.title: The Kan Data Migration Adjoint Triple Triangle

### Global Section Synthesis: The Sheaf of Ologged Concepts ($\mathcal{O} : \text{Open}(\mathcal{X})^{\text{op}} \to \mathbf{Sch} \simeq \mathbf{Cat}$)

In a conventional **flat knowledge graph**, nodes and edges are global, context-free triples: if two chapters or experts use different terminology, or if a statement only holds under specific hypotheses, a flat graph either collapses them into a contradiction or fragments into disconnected islands without composition laws `[p. 11–13, Fig 1.1]`.

Spivak replaces flat graphs with a **three-tiered categorical sheaf architecture** culminating in **Section 7.2.3.11 (*Sheaf of ologged concepts*, `[p. 523–524]`)**:

1. **Local Worldviews as Ologs / Schemas ($\mathcal{O}(v) \in \mathbf{Sch} \simeq \mathbf{Cat}$):**
   Each local domain, chapter, or agent $v$ holds a rigorous **olog** (Ontology Log) `[p. 47–67, Sec 2.3]`, where every box is a set-valued **Type**, every arrow is a deterministic **Functional Aspect**, and every declared **Fact** is a **commutative diagram (path equivalence $p \simeq q$)** `[p. 252, Def 4.5.2.3]`. By **Theorem $\mathbf{Cat} \simeq \mathbf{Sch}$** `[p. 379–391, Sec 5.4]`, each local olog is a category.

2. **The Simplicial Base Complex $X$ & Alexandrov Topology $\text{Alx}(X^{\text{op}})$:**
   Let $X$ be a **simplicial complex** `[p. 144, Sec 3.4.4.3; p. 523]` whose vertices $v \in X_0$ represent individual conceptual domains (or people/experts) and whose higher simplices $u \in X_n$ represent multi-domain overlaps. Ordering simplices by inclusion $u \subseteq v$ makes $X$ a **preorder** `[p. 223, Def 4.4.1.1]`. Applying the **Alexandrov functor** $\text{Alx} : \mathbf{PrO} \to \mathbf{Top}$ to $X^{\text{op}}$ produces a topological space $\mathcal{X} = \text{Alx}(X^{\text{op}})$ whose open sets are unions of simplices `[p. 524]`.

3. **Restriction Morphisms ($\rho_{v,u} : \mathcal{O}(v) \to \mathcal{O}(u)$) & Descent Data ($p_{i,j}$):**
   Whenever simplex $u \subseteq v$, there is a **schema morphism** $\rho_{v,u} : \mathcal{O}(v) \to \mathcal{O}(u)$ extracting the common-ground worldview shared by all members of $v$ `[p. 523]`. When two domains $G_1, G_2$ describe the same phenomenon using different vocabulary on their overlap $H = G_1 \cap G_2$, **Descent Data** $p_{1,2} : \mathcal{O}_1|_H \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}_2|_H$ `[p. 521, Remark 7.2.3.6; p. 524, Ex 7.2.3.12]` translates isomorphically between them.

4. **The Sheaf Gluing Condition (`[p. 520–521, Def 7.2.3.5]`):**
   Given an open cover $U = \bigcup_{i=1}^n V_i$ of conceptual domains, local claims or data assignments $a_i \in \mathcal{O}(V_i)$ that agree on all pairwise overlaps ($a_i|_{V_i \cap V_j} = a_j|_{V_i \cap V_j}$) glue uniquely into a **single coherent Global Section $b \in \mathcal{O}(U)$** via the fiber product $\mathcal{O}(V_1 \cup V_2) \cong \mathcal{O}(V_1) \times_{\mathcal{O}(V_1 \cap V_2)} \mathcal{O}(V_2)$ `[p. 520, p. 522 App 7.2.3.9]`.

### Global Section Synthesis: Categorical Databases ($\mathbf{Cat} \simeq \mathbf{Sch}$) & The Adjoint Migration Triple ($\Sigma_F \dashv \Delta_F \dashv \Pi_F$)

Spivak demonstrates that relational databases and category theory are not merely analogous—they are **mathematically equivalent**:

1. **Schemas Present Categories ($\mathbf{Cat} \simeq \mathbf{Sch}$, `[p. 252–266, p. 379–391]`):**
   - A **database schema** $\mathcal{C} = (G, \simeq)$ consists of a directed graph $G = (V, A, \text{src}, \text{tgt})$ of tables ($V$) and foreign-key columns ($A$), together with a **path equivalence declaration (congruence $\simeq$)** on $\text{Path}(G)$ specifying which composite foreign-key chains must be equal `[p. 253, Def 4.5.2.3]`.
   - Quotienting the free path category $\text{Path}(G)$ by $\simeq$ yields a small category $L(\mathcal{C}) \in \mathbf{Cat}$ `[p. 318, Sec 5.2.2]`. Conversely, every small category $\mathcal{C}$ has an underlying graph $R(\mathcal{C})$ whose composition table defines a canonical congruence. In **Section 5.4.2 (`[p. 386–391]`)**, Spivak proves $L : \mathbf{Sch} \simeq \mathbf{Cat} : R$ is an **equivalence of categories**.

2. **Database Instances Are $\mathbf{Set}$-Valued Functors ($I : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$, `[p. 261, p. 364]`):**
   - Populating a schema $\mathcal{C}$ with data assigns a set of rows $I(c)$ to each table $c \in \text{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$ and a function $I(f) : I(c) \to I(c')$ to each foreign key $f : c \to c'$ such that path equations hold—which is *precisely* a functor $I : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ `[p. 290, Prop 5.1.2.10]`.
   - Morphisms between database instances are **natural transformations** $\alpha : I \Rightarrow J$, forming the functor category $\mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Inst} = \mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$ `[p. 364, Def 5.3.3.1]`.

3. **The Adjoint Triple of Data Migration (`[p. 481–492, Sec 7.1.4]`):**
   Given a schema translation functor $F : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$, how do we migrate data between $\mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$ and $\mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$?
   - **Pullback Migration $\Delta_F : \mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathbf{Set} \to \mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$ (`[p. 481, Def 7.1.4.1]`):** Defined by precomposition $\Delta_F(J) = J \circ F$. It restricts a $\mathcal{D}$-instance along $F$ (just like a sheaf restriction map $\rho_{U,V}$!).
   - **Left Kan Migration $\Sigma_F : \mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set} \to \mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$ ($\Sigma_F \dashv \Delta_F$, `[p. 483, Prop 7.1.4.4]`):** The *liberal* pushforward. It takes **colimits (disjoint unions / quotients)** over the comma category $(F \downarrow d)$ and freely invents **labeled Skolem nulls** when foreign keys are missing `[p. 485, Ex 7.1.4.7]`.
   - **Right Kan Migration $\Pi_F : \mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set} \to \mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}$ ($\Delta_F \dashv \Pi_F$, `[p. 483, Prop 7.1.4.4]`):** The *conservative* pushforward. It takes **limits (fiber products / SQL inner joins / filters)** over $(d \downarrow F)$, keeping only compatible tuples that satisfy all target constraints `[p. 489, Ex 7.1.4.9]`.

### Global Section Synthesis: Universal Limits ($\varprojlim D$) vs. Universal Colimits ($\varinjlim D$)

Limits and colimits are exact categorical duals (`[p. 439, Sec 6.2.1]`): a colimit of $D : J \to \mathcal{C}$ is a limit of $D^{\text{op}} : J^{\text{op}} \to \mathcal{C}^{\text{op}}$. Yet in $\mathbf{Set}$ and scientific modeling, they play complementary operational roles:

| Dimension | Universal Limits ($\varprojlim_J D$) | Universal Colimits ($\varinjlim_J D$) |
|---|---|---|
| **Universal Geometry** | **Terminal Cone** $(L, \pi_j : L \to D(j))$ receiving a unique map *from* any cone $W$ `[p. 418, Def 6.1.3.2]` | **Initial Cocone** $(C, \iota_j : D(j) \to C)$ sending a unique map *to* any cocone $W$ `[p. 429, Def 6.1.3.17]` |
| **Operational Action in $\mathbf{Set}$** | **Equationally Constrained Subsets of Tuples** (carving out compatible states inside $\prod_j D(j)$) | **Quotients of Disjoint Unions** (gluing pieces $\bigsqcup_j D(j)$ together along shared overlaps $\sim$) |
| **Empty Diagram ($J = \varnothing$)** | **Terminal Object** $\{\star\}$ (1-element singleton set) `[p. 108, Def 3.2.3.5]` | **Initial Object** $\varnothing$ (empty set) `[p. 126, Def 3.3.3.5]` |
| **Discrete Pair ($J = \{\bullet, \bullet\}$)** | **Product** $X \times Y = \{(x,y)\}$ `[p. 72, Def 3.1.1.1]` | **Coproduct** $X \sqcup Y$ (disjoint union) `[p. 80, Def 3.1.2.1]` |
| **3-Object Overlap** | **Pullback (Fiber Product)** $X \times_Z Y = \{(x,y) \mid f(x)=g(y)\}$ over cospan $X \xrightarrow{f} Z \xleftarrow{g} Y$ `[p. 90, Def 3.2.1.1]` | **Pushout** $X \sqcup_W Y = (X \sqcup Y)/(f(w) \sim g(w))$ under span $X \xleftarrow{f} W \xrightarrow{g} Y$ `[p. 118, Def 3.3.2.1]` |
| **Parallel Pair ($J = \bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet$)** | **Equalizer** $\text{Eq}(f,g) = \{x \in X \mid f(x)=g(x)\}$ `[p. 107, Def 3.2.3.1]` | **Coequalizer** $\text{Coeq}(f,g) = Y/(f(x) \sim g(x))$ `[p. 125, Def 3.3.3.1]` |
| **Adjoint Preservation (`[p. 478]` )**| Preserved by **Right Adjoints** (**RAPL**: $\Pi_F$, forgetful functors) | Preserved by **Left Adjoints** (**LAPC**: $\Sigma_F$, free functors) |
| **Role in Sheaf Theory (`[p. 520]` )**| **Global Sections** $\mathcal{O}(U)$ are the **limit (equalizer)** of local sections $\prod \mathcal{O}(V_i) \rightrightarrows \prod \mathcal{O}(V_i \cap V_j)$ | **Open Cover** $U = \bigcup V_i$ is the **colimit (join)** of subregions $V_i$ over intersections $V_i \cap V_j$ |

notebook_investigations.synthesis_markdown:
### Global Section Synthesis: Resolving the Scientific Method Cycle via Monads ($T$) & Kleisli Categories ($\mathbf{Set}_T$)

One of the deepest narrative arcs spanning Spivak's entire 609-page book begins on **Page 11 (`Figure 1.1`)** and concludes on **Page 544 (`Example 7.3.3.10`)**:

1. **The Chapter 1 Obstruction (`[p. 11–13, Fig 1.1]`):**
   On page 11, Spivak draws the classic cycle of the scientific method:
   $$\text{Observation} \xrightarrow{\text{analyzed by person}} \text{Hypothesis} \xrightarrow{\text{analyzed by person}} \text{Prediction} \xrightarrow{\text{motivates}} \text{Experiment} \xrightarrow{\text{executed}} \text{Observation}$$
   He immediately points out a **sheaf/olog obstruction**: in $\mathbf{Set}$, every olog arrow must be a *deterministic function* (`[p. 52, Rules 2.3.2.1]`). Yet a prediction does *not* uniquely determine an experiment—an expert might design one experiment on Monday and a different one on Tuesday, and executing an experiment depends on laboratory conditions and noise!

2. **Monads Formalize Implicit Context (`[p. 527–539, Sec 7.3.1–7.3.2]`):**
   A **monad** $(T, \eta, \mu)$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ `[p. 533, Def 7.3.2.1]` consists of:
   - An endofunctor $T : \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ that wraps any output type $Y$ in its contextual envelope $T(Y)$ (such as partiality $Y \sqcup \{\☺\}$ `[p. 529, Ex 7.3.1.1]`, powerset non-determinism $\mathbb{P}(Y)$, probability distributions $\text{Dist}(Y)`[p. 537, Ex 7.3.2.6]`, or reader/state context $(Y \times E)^E$).
   - A **unit** $\eta_X : X \to T(X)$ injecting context-free values, and a **multiplication** $\mu_X : T(T(X)) \to T(X)$ flattening sequential contexts.

3. **The Kleisli Category $\mathbf{Set}_T$ (`[p. 540–545, Sec 7.3.3]`):**
   In the **Kleisli category** $\mathbf{Set}_T$ `[p. 540, Def 7.3.3.1]`, the objects are ordinary sets, but a morphism $f : X \to Y$ in $\mathbf{Set}_T$ is an actual function $f : X \to T(Y)$ in $\mathbf{Set}$! Two contextual arrows $f : X \to T(Y)$ and $g : Y \to T(Z)$ compose via:
   $$g \circ_K f = \mu_Z \circ T(g) \circ f : X \to T(Z)$$

4. **Resolution in Example 7.3.3.10 (`[p. 544–545]`):**
   By modeling the scientific expert, historical background, and experimental apparatus as a monad $T$, every arrow in **Figure 1.1** (`Prediction -> Experiment`, `Experiment -> Observation`) becomes a legitimate deterministic morphism inside the **Kleisli category $\mathbf{Set}_T$** (`Figure 7.3, p. 544`)! What failed to glue in context-free $\mathbf{Set}$ glues into an exact global section once the monadic context $T$ is made explicit.

notebook_investigations.synthesis_markdown:
### Global Section Synthesis: Perspective (Yoneda), Fibred Flattening ($\int I$), and Hierarchical Operads ($\mathcal{O}$)

Together, these three pillars of Chapters 6 and 7 answer how objects are defined by relationships, how schemas relate to instance graphs, and how multi-part systems assemble across scales:

1. **Representable Functors & Yoneda's Lemma (`[p. 505–508, Sec 7.2.1.3]`):**
   - For any object $c \in \text{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$, the **representable functor** $Y_c = \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(c, -) : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ `[p. 505, Def 7.2.1.14]` records how $c$ sees every object $d \in \mathcal{C}$ via outgoing paths.
   - **Yoneda's Lemma (`[p. 506]`):** For any instance/functor $I : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$, there is a canonical bijection:
     $$\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}\text{-}\mathbf{Set}}(Y_c, I) \cong I(c)$$
     given by evaluating a natural transformation $\alpha : Y_c \Rightarrow I$ at the identity morphism $\text{id}_c \in Y_c(c)$. Thus, an object $c$ is completely determined (up to unique isomorphism) by its web of morphisms to all other objects!

2. **The Grothendieck Construction / Category of Elements ($\int_{\mathcal{C}} I \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{C}$, `[p. 444–450, Sec 6.2.2]`):**
   - Given a database instance or presheaf $I : \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$, how do we view all rows across all tables as a single unified graph without losing schema typing?
   - **Definition 6.2.2.1 (`[p. 444]`):** The **category of elements** $\int I$ has objects $(c, x)$ where $c \in \text{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$ and $x \in I(c)$, and morphisms $f : (c, x) \to (c', x')$ whenever $f : c \to c'$ satisfies $I(f)(x) = x'$.
   - In **Application 6.2.2.5 (`[p. 447]`)**, Spivak shows that $\int I$ is the exact mathematical bridge to **RDF triple stores**: the functor $\pi : \int I \to \mathcal{C}$ equips every RDF node $(c,x)$ with its rigorous schema stalk $c$.

3. **Operads & Hierarchical Self-Similarity (`[p. 557–581, Sec 7.4]`):**
   - Categories only have 1-input, 1-output arrows $f : x \to y$. **Operads (`[p. 559, Def 7.4.1.1]`)** generalize categories to **multi-input wiring morphisms** $\phi \in \mathcal{O}(x_1, \dots, x_n; y)$ that nest recursively (`[p. 580, Fig 7.6]`).
   - An **operad algebra** $A : \mathcal{O} \to \mathbf{Set}$ `[p. 567, Def 7.4.2.1]` assigns a state space $A(x)$ to each module interface and a composition law $A(\phi) : A(x_1) \times \dots \times A(x_n) \to A(y)$ assembling micro-scale behaviors (e.g., tropocollagen molecules $\to$ fibrils $\to$ tendon fibers `[p. 581, Fig 7.7]`, or sub-agents in an AI architecture) into macro-scale system invariants.

formal_items.text: Notation 2.1.1.1. The symbol ∅ denotes the set with no elements (see Figure 2.1), which can also be written as { }. The symbol ℕ denotes the set of natural numbers: ℕ≔{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, …, 877,…}. (2.1) The symbol ℤ denotes the set of integers, which contains both the natural numbers and their negatives, ℤ≔{…,−551,…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…}. (2.2) If A and B are sets, we say that A is a subset of B, and write A ⊆ B, if every element of A is an element of B. So we have ℕ ⊆ ℤ. Checking the definition, one sees that for any set A, we have (perhaps uninteresting) subsets ∅ ⊆ A and A ⊆ A. We can use set-builder notation to denote subsets. For example, the set of even integers can be written {n ∈ ℤ | n is even}. The set of integers greater than 2 can

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Let {1 3} What are all
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.1.2. Let A ≔ {1, 2, 3}. What are all the subsets of A? Hint: There are eight. A set can have other sets as elements. For example, the set X≔{{1,2},{4},{1,3,6}} has three elements, each of which is a set.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Given function we think of as
formal_items.text: Slogan 2.1.2.1. Given a function f : X → Y, we think of X as a set of things, and Y as a set of bins. The function tells us in which bin to put each thing.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — In studying the mechanics of materials
formal_items.text: Application 2.1.2.2. In studying the mechanics of materials, one wishes to know how a material responds to tension. For example, a rubber band responds to tension differently than a spring does. To each material we can associate a force- extension curve, recording how much force the material carries when extended to various lengths. Once we fix a methodology for performing experiments, finding a material’s force-extension curve would ideally constitute a function from the set of materials to the set of curves.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Here is simplified account of how
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.3. Here is a simplified account of how the brain receives light. The eye contains about 100 million photoreceptor (PR) cells. Each connects to a retinal ganglion (RG) cell. No PR cell connects to two different RG cells, but usually many PR cells can attach to a single RG cell. Let PR denote the set of photoreceptor cells, and let RG denote the set of retinal ganglion cells. a. According to the above account, does the connection pattern constitute a function RG → PR, a function PR → RG, or neither one? b. Would you guess that the connection pattern that exists between other areas of the brain are function-like? Justify your answer.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Suppose that is set and X′
formal_items.text: Example 2.1.2.4. Suppose that X is a set and X′ ⊆ X is a subset. Then we can consider the function X′ → X given by sending every element of X′ to “itself” as an element of X. For example, if X = {a, b, c, d, e, f} and X′ = {b, d, e}, then X′ ⊆ X. We turn that into the function X′ → X given by b ↦ b, d ↦ d, e ↦ e.2 As a matter of notation, we may sometimes say the following: Let X be a set, and let i : X′ ⊆ X be a subset. Here we are making clear that X′ is a subset of X, but that i is the name of the associated function.

formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.5. Let f : ℕ → ℕ be the function that sends every natural number to its square, e.g., f(6) = 36. First fill in the blanks, then answer a question. a. 2 ↦ ________ b. 0 ↦ ________ c. −2 ↦ ________ d. 5 ↦ ________ e. Consider the symbol → and the symbol ↦. What is the difference between how these two symbols are used so far in this book? formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.6. If f : X → Y is depicted by Figure 2.2, write its image, im(f) as a set. Given a function f : X → Y and a function g : Y → Z, where the codomain of f is the same set as the domain of g (namely, Y), we say that f and g are composable X→fY→gZ. The composition of f and g is denoted by g ○ f : X → Z. See Figure 2.3.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Given composable functions X→fY→gZ we have
formal_items.text: Slogan 2.1.2.7. Given composable functions X→fY→gZ, we have a way of putting every thing in X into a bin in Y, and we have a way of putting each bin from Y into a larger bin in Z. The composite, g ○ f : X → Z, is the resulting way that every thing in X is put into a bin in Z.

formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.8. Figure 2.3 Functions f : X → Y and g : Y → Z compose to a function g ○ f : X → Z (follow the arrows). If A ⊆ X is a subset, Example 2.1.2.4 showed how to think of it as a function i : A → X. Given a function f : X → Y, we can compose A→iX→fY and get a

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — By definition of image see 2.3
formal_items.text: Solution 2.1.2.8. By definition of image (see (2.3), we have f(A)={y∈ℤ|∃a∈A such that f○i(a)=y}. Since A = {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3} and since i(a) = a for all a ∈ A, we have f(A) = {0, 1, 4, 9}. Note that an element of a set can only be in the set once; even though f(−1) = f(1) = 1, we need only mention 1 once in f(A). In other words, if a student has an answer such as {1, 0, 1, 4, 9}, this suggests a minor confusion.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Let be set and an element
formal_items.text: Notation 2.1.2.9. Let X be a set and x ∈ X an element. There is a function {☺} → X that sends ☺ ↦ x. We say that this function represents x ∈ X. We may denote it x: {☺} → X.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Let be set let be an
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.10. Let X be a set, let x ∈ X be an element, and let x: {☺} → X be the function representing it. Given a function f : X → Y, what is f ○ x?

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Suppose given sets and functions A→fB→gC
formal_items.text: Remark 2.1.2.11. Suppose given sets A, B, C and functions A→fB→gC. The classical order for writing their composition has been used so far, namely, g ○ f : A → C. For any element a ∈ A, we write g ○ f(a) to mean g(f(a)). This means “do g to whatever results from doing f to a.” However, there is another way to write this composition, called diagrammatic order. Instead of g ○ f, we would write f; g : A → C, meaning “do f, then do g.” Given an element a ∈ A, represented by a: {☺} → A, we have an element a; f; g. Let X and Y be sets. We write HomSet(X, Y) to denote the set of functions X → Y.3 Note that two functions f, g : X → Y are equal if and only if for every element x ∈ X, we have f(x) = g(x).

formal_items.title: Sets and functions
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.12.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Find set such that for all
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.13. a. Find a set A such that for all sets X there is exactly one element in HomSet(X, A). Hint: Draw a picture of proposed A’s and X’s. How many dots should be in A? b. Find a set B such that for all sets X there is exactly one element in HomSet(B, X).

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Here is one {☺} Here is
formal_items.text: Solution 2.1.2.13. a. Here is one: A ≔ {☺}. (Here is another, A ≔ {48}, and another, A ≔ {a1}). Why? We are trying to count the number of functions X → A. Regardless of X and A, in order to give a function X → A one must answer the question, Where do I send x? several times, once for each element x ∈ X. Each element of X is sent to an element in A. For example, if X = {1, 2, 3}, then one asks three questions: Where do I send 1? Where do I send 2? Where do I send 3? When A has only one element, there is only one place to send each x. A function X → {☺} would be written 1 ↦ ☺, 2 ↦ ☺, 3 ↦ ☺. There is only one such function, so HomSet(X, {☺}) has one element. b. B = ∅ is the only possibility.

formal_items.title: Isomorphism
formal_items.text: Definition 2.1.2.14 (Isomorphism). Let X and Y be sets. A function f : X → Y is called an isomorphism, denoted f : X→≅Y, if there exists a function g : Y → X such that g ○ f = idX and f ○ g = idY. Figure 2.4 An isomorphism X→≅Y.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — If and are sets and is
formal_items.text: Example 2.1.2.15. If X and Y are sets and f : X → Y is an isomorphism, then the analogue of Figure 2.2 will look like a perfect matching, more often called a one- to-one correspondence. That means that no two arrows will hit the same element of Y, and every element of Y will be in the image. For example, Figure 2.4 depicts an isomorphism X→≅Y between four element sets.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — There is an isomorphism between the
formal_items.text: Application 2.1.2.16. There is an isomorphism between the set NucDNA of nucleotides found in DNA and the set NucRNA of nucleotides found in RNA. Indeed, both sets have four elements, so there are 24 different isomorphisms. But only one is useful in biology. Before we say which one it is, let us say there is also an isomorphism NucDNA ≅ {A, C, G, T} and an isomorphism NucRNA ≅ {A, C, G, U}, and we will use the letters as abbreviations for the nucleotides. The convenient isomorphism NucDNA→≅NucRNA is that given by RNA transcription; it sends A↦U, C↦G, G↦C, T↦A. (See also

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — There is also an isomorphism NucDNA→≅NucDNA
formal_items.text: Application 5.1.2.21.) There is also an isomorphism NucDNA→≅NucDNA (the matching in the double helix), given by A↦T, C↦G, G↦C, T↦A. Protein production can be modeled as a function from the set of 3-nucleotide sequences to the set of eukaryotic amino acids. However, it cannot be an isomorphism because there are 43 = 64 triplets of RNA nucleotides but only 21 eukaryotic amino acids.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Let be natural number and let
formal_items.text: Exercise 2.1.2.17. Let n ∈ ℕ be a natural number, and let X be a set with exactly n elements. a. How many isomorphisms are there from X to itself? b. Does your formula from part (a) hold when n = 0?

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — The following facts hold about isomorphism
formal_items.text: Proposition 2.1.2.18. The following facts hold about isomorphism. 1. Any set A is isomorphic to itself; i.e., there exists an isomorphism A→≅A. 2. For any sets A and B, if A is isomorphic to B, then B is isomorphic to A.

Cardinality of finite sets
formal_items.text: Definition 2.1.2.23 (Cardinality of finite sets). Let A be a set and n ∈ ℕ a natural number. We say that A has cardinality n, denoted |A|=n, if there exists an isomorphism of sets A ≅ n. If there exists some n ∈ ℕ such that A has cardinality n, then we say that A is finite. Otherwise, we say that A is infinite and write |A| ∞.

We will see in Corollary 3.4.5.6 that for any m, n ∈ ℕ, there is an isomorphism m ≅ n if and only if m = n. So if we find that A has cardinality m and that A has cardinality n, then m = n.

formal_items.title: Sets and functions — Let and be finite sets If
formal_items.text: Proposition 2.1.2.25. Let A and B be finite sets. If there is an isomorphism of sets f : A → B, then the two sets have the same cardinality, |A| = |B|. Proof. If f : A → B is an isomorphism and B ≅ n, then A ≅ n because the composition of two isomorphisms is an isomorphism.

formal_items.title: Ologs — The author of an olog has
formal_items.text: Warning 2.3.2.2. The author of an olog has a worldview, some fragment of which is captured in the olog. When person A examines the olog of person B, person A may or may not agree with it. For example, person B may have the following olog which associates to each marriage a man and a woman. Person A may take the position that some marriages involve two men or two women and thus see B’s olog as wrong. Such disputes are not “problems” with either A’s olog or B’s olog; they are discrepancies between worldviews. Hence, a reader R may see an olog in this book and notice a discrepancy between R’s worldview and my own, but this is not a problem with the olog. Rules are enforced to ensure that an olog is structurally sound, not to ensure that it “correctly reflects reality,” since worldviews can differ. Consider the aspect ⌜an object⌝→has⌜a weight⌝. At some point in history, this would have been considered a valid function. Now we know that the same object would have a different weight on the moon than it has on earth. Thus, as worldviews change, we often need to add more information to an olog. Even the validity of ⌜an object on earth⌝→has⌜a weight⌝ is questionable, e.g., if I am considered to be the same object on earth before and after I eat Thanksgiving dinner. However, to build a model we need to choose a level of granularity and try to stay within it, or the whole model would evap

formal_items.text: Remark 2.3.2.3. In keeping with Warning 2.3.2.2, the arrows in (2.12*) and (2.13*) may not be wrong but simply reflect that the author has an idiosyncratic worldview or vocabulary. Maybe the author believes that every mechanical pencil uses exactly one piece of lead. If this is so, then ⌜a mechanical pencil⌝→uses⌜a piece of lead⌝ is indeed a valid aspect. Similarly, suppose the author meant to say that each person was once a child, or that a person has an inner child. Since every person has one and only one inner child (according to the author), the map ⌜a person⌝→has as inner child⌜a child⌝ is a valid aspect. We cannot fault the olog for its author’s view, but note that we have changed the name of the label to make the intention more explicit. 2.3.2.4 Reading aspects and paths as English phrases Each arrow (aspect) X→fY can be read by first reading the label on its source box X, then the label on the arrow f, and finally the label on its target box Y. formal_items.title: Piecewise defined curves
formal_items.text: Application 3.1.2.10 (Piecewise defined curves). In science, curves are often defined or considered piecewise. For example, in testing the mechanical properties of a material, we might be interested in various regions of deformation, such as elastic, plastic, or post-fracture. These are three intervals on which the material displays different kinds of properties. For real numbers a b ∈ ℝ, let [a, b] ≔ {x ∈ ℝ | a x b} denote the closed interval. Given a function [a, b]→fℝ and a function [c, d]→gℝ, the universal property for coproducts implies that they extend uniquely to a function [a, b] ⊔ [c, d] → ℝ, which will appear as a piecewise defined curve, {fg(x)={f(x)if x∈[a, b],g(x)if x∈[c, d]. Often we are given a curve on [a, b] and another on [b, c], where the two curves agree at the point b. This situation is described by pushouts, which are mild generalizations of coproducts (see Section 3.3.2).

formal_items.title: Equivalence relations and equivalence classes
formal_items.text: Definition 3.3.1.1 (Equivalence relations and equivalence classes). Let X be a set, and consider the product X × X, as in Definition 3.1.1.1. An equivalence relation on X is a subset R ⊆ X × X satisfying the following properties for all x, y, z ∈ X: Reflexivity: (x, x) ∈ R; Symmetry: (x, y) ∈ R if and only if (y, x) ∈ R; Transitivity: If (x, y) ∈ R and (y, z) ∈ R, then (x, z) ∈ R. If R is an equivalence relation, we often write x ∼R y, or simply x ∼ y, to mean (x, y) ∈ R. For convenience we may refer to the equivalence relation by the symbol ∼, saying that ∼ is an equivalence relation on X. An equivalence class of ∼ is a subset A ⊆ X such that A is nonempty, A ≠ ∅; if x ∈ A, then y ∈ A if and only if x ∼ y. Suppose that ∼ is an equivalence relation on X. The quotient of X by ∼, denoted X/ ∼, is the set of equivalence classes of ∼. By definition, for any element x ∈ X, there is exactly one equivalence class A such that x ∈ A. Thus we can define a function Q: X → X/∼, called the quotient function, sending each element x ∈ X to the equivalence class containing it. Note that for any y ∈ X/∼, there is some x ∈ X with Q(x) = y; we call x a representative of the equivalence class y.

formal_items.title: Finite colimits in Set — Let denote the set of integers
formal_items.text: Example 3.3.1.2. Let ℤ denote the set of integers. Define a relation R ⊆ ℤ × ℤ by R={(x,y)|∃n∈ℤ such that x+7n=y}. Then R is an equivalence relation because x + 7 * 0 = x (reflexivity); x + 7 * n = y if and only if y + 7 * (−n) = x (symmetry); and x + 7n = y and y + 7m = z together imply that x + 7(m + n) = z (transitivity). An example equivalence class A ⊆ ℤ for this relation is A = {…, −12, −5, 2, 9, …}.

formal_items.title: Partitions
formal_items.text: Example 3.3.1.4 (Partitions). An equivalence relation on a set X can be thought of as a way of partitioning X. A partition of X consists of a set I, called the set of parts, and for every element i ∈ I, the selection of a subset Xi ⊆ X such that two properties hold: Every element x ∈ X is in some part (i.e., for all x ∈ X, there exists i ∈ I such that x ∈ Xi). No element can be found in two different parts (i.e., if x ∈ Xi and x ∈ Xj, then i = j). Given a partition of X, we define an equivalence relation ∼ on X by putting x ∼ x′ if x and x′ are in the same part (i.e., if there exists i ∈ I such that x, x′ ∈ Xi). The parts become the equivalence classes of this relation. Conversely, given an equivalence relation, one makes a partition on X by taking I to be the set of equivalence classes and, for each i ∈ I, letting Xi be the elements in that equivalence class.

formal_items.title: Generating equivalence relations
formal_items.text: Proposition 3.3.1.7 (Generating equivalence relations). Let X be a set and R ⊆ X × X any subset. There exists a relation S ⊆ X × X such that S is an equivalence relation; R ⊆ S; for any equivalence relation S′ such that R ⊆ S′, we have S ⊆ S′. The relation S′ is called the equivalence relation generated by R. Proof. Let LR be the set of all equivalence relations on X that contain R. In other words, each element ℓ ∈ LR is an equivalence relation, so we have R ⊆ ℓ ⊆ X × X. The set LR is nonempty because X × X ⊆ X × X is an equivalence relation containing R. Let S denote the set of pairs (x1, x2) ∈ X × X that appear in every element of LR, that is, S=∩ℓ∈LRℓ. Note that R ⊆ S by definition. We need only show that S is an equivalence relation. Clearly, S is reflexive, because each ℓ ∈ LR is. If (x, y) ∈ S, then (x, y) ∈ ℓ for all ℓ ∈ LR. But since each ℓ is an equivalence relation, (y, x) ∈ ℓ too, so (y, x) ∈ S. This shows that S is symmetric. The proof that it is transitive is similar: if (x, y) ∈ S and (y, z) ∈ S, then they are both in each ℓ, which puts (x, z) in each ℓ, which puts it in S.

formal_items.title: Finite colimits in Set — Node is equivalent to node if
formal_items.text: Solution 3.3.1.11. a. Node x is equivalent to node y if and only if one can get from x to y by moving along some finite number of edges (including no edges if x = y). In other words, if nodes are street addresses in a city, and each edge is like a street, then two addresses are equivalent if a pedestrian can get from one to the other. b. It is called the set of “connected components” of the network. Think of a connected component as an island within the network. A pedestrian can get from everywhere on the island to everywhere else on the island but cannot get off the island.

formal_items.title: Finite colimits in Set — has the benefit of working even
formal_items.text: Proposition 3.3.1.7 has the benefit of working even if |X| ∞, but it has the cost that it is not very intuitive nor useful in practice when X is finite. The intuitive way to think about the idea of equivalence relation generated by R is as follows: 1. First add to R what is demanded by reflexivity, R1 ≔ R ∪ {(x, x) | x ∈ X}. 2. To the result, add what is demanded by symmetry, R2 ≔ R1 ∪{(x, y) | (y, x) ∈ R1}. 3. Finally, to the result, add what is demanded by transitivity, S=R2∪{(x,z)|(x,y)∈R2,and (y,z)∈R2}. Then S is an equivalence relation, the smallest one containing R.

formal_items.title: Pushout
formal_items.text: Example 3.3.2.3 (Pushout). In ologs (3.17) and (3.18) right-hand diagram is a pushout of the left-hand diagram. The new object, D, is the union of B and C, but instances of A are equated to their B and C aspects. In diagram (3.17), the two arrows in the left-hand olog are inclusions: its author considers every cell in the shoulder to be both part of the arm and part of the torso. The pushout is then the union. In olog (3.17), the shoulder is seen as part of the arm and part of the torso. When taking the union of these two parts, we do not want to double-count cells in the shoulder (as would be done in the coproduct B ⊔ C; see Example 3.1.2.14). Thus we create a new type A for cells in the shoulder, which are considered the same whether viewed as cells in the arm or cells in the torso. In general, if one wishes to take two things and glue them together, with A as the glue and B and C as the two things to be glued, the result is the pushout B ⊔A C. (A nice image of this can be seen in the setting of topological spaces; see Example 6.1.3.39.)

formal_items.title: Other notions in Set — summarizes some properties of products coprod
formal_items.text: Proposition 3.4.3.1 summarizes some properties of products, coproducts, and exponentials, and shows them all in a familiar light, namely, that of elementary school arithmetic. In fact, one can think of the natural numbers as literally being the isomorphism classes of finite sets—that is what they are used for in counting. Consider the standard procedure for counting the elements of a set S, say, cows in a field. One points to an element in S and simultaneously says “one”, points to another element in S and simultaneously says “two”, and so on until finished. By pointing at a cow as you speak a number, you are drawing an imaginary line between the number and the cow. In other words, this procedure amounts to nothing more than creating an isomorphism (one-to-one mapping) between S and some set {1, 2, 3, …, n}. Again, the natural numbers are the isomorphism classes of finite sets. Their behavior, i.e., the arithmetic of natural numbers, reflects the behavior of sets. For example, the fact that multiplication distributes over addition is a fact about grids of dots, as in Example 3.1.1.2. The following proposition lays out such arithmetic properties of sets. This proposition denotes the coproduct of two sets A and B by the notation A + B rather than A ⊔ B. It is a reasonable notation in general, and one that is often used.

formal_items.title: Other notions in Set — Let be set let ℙ(V be
formal_items.text: Definition 3.4.4.4. Let V be a set, let ℙ(V) be its power-set. Since each element x ∈ ℙ(V) is a subset x ⊆ U, we can make sense of the expression x ⊆ x′ for x, x′ ∈ ℙ(V). A subset X ⊆ ℙ(V) is called downward-closed if for every u ∈ X and every u′ ⊆ u, we have u′ ∈ X. We say that X contains all atoms if for every v ∈ V, the singleton set {v} is an element of X. A simplicial complex is a pair (V, X), where V is a set and X ⊆ ℙ(V) is a downward-closed subset that contains all atoms. The elements of X are called simplices (singular: simplex). Any subset u ⊆ V has a cardinality |u|, so we have a function X → ℕ sending each simplex to its cardinality. The set of simplices with cardinality n + 1 is denoted Xn, and each element x ∈ Xn is called an n-simplex.7 Since X contains all atoms (subsets of cardinality 1), we have an isomorphism X0 ≅ V, and we may also call the 0-simplices vertices. We sometimes call the 1- simplices edges.8 Since X0 ≅ V, a simplicial complex (V, X) may simply be denoted X.

formal_items.text: Proposition 3.4.5.4. A function f : X → Y is bijective if and only if it is an isomorphism. Proof. Suppose that f is bijective; we define an inverse g : Y → X. For each y ∈ Y, the preimage f−1(y) ⊆ X is a set with exactly one element. Indeed, it has at least one element because f is surjective, and it has at most one element because f is injective. Define g(y) to be the unique element of f−1(y). It is easy to see that f and g are mutually inverse. Note that for every set X, the identity function idX : X → X is bijective. Suppose now that f is an isomorphism, and let g be its inverse. The composition g ○ f = idX is injective, and the composition f ○ g = idY is surjective, so f is injective and surjective by Exercise 3.4.5.3.

If m > n, then n + 1 m, and we have already shown that there exists an injection g : n + 1 ↪ m. Composing, we have an injection h ≔ g ○ f : n + 1 ↪ n by Exercise 3.4.5.3. One can show by induction on n that this is impossible.

formal_items.title: Monoids — The performance of sequence of several
formal_items.text: Slogan 4.1.0.14. The performance of a sequence of several actions is itself the performance of an action—a more complex action, but an action nonetheless. Mathematical objects called monoids and groups are tasked with encoding the agent’s perspective, i.e., what the agent can do, and what happens when she does a sequence of actions in succession. A monoid can be construed as a set of actions together with a formula that encodes how a sequence of actions is itself considered an action. A group is the same as a monoid except that every action is required to be reversible.

formal_items.title: Monoid
formal_items.text: Definition 4.1.1.1 (Monoid). A monoid is a sequence (M, e, ⋆), where M is a set, e ∈ M is an element, and ⋆: M × M → M is a function, such that the following monoid laws hold for all m, n, p ∈ M: m ⋆ e = m. e ⋆ m = m. (m ⋆ n) ⋆ p = m ⋆ (n ⋆ p). We refer to e as the unit element and to ⋆ as the multiplication formula for the monoid.1 We call the first two rules unit laws and the third rule the associativity law for monoids.

formal_items.title: Monoids — To be pedantic the conditions from
formal_items.text: Remark 4.1.1.2. To be pedantic, the conditions from Definition 4.1.1.1 should be stated ⋆(m, e) = m. ⋆(e, m) = m. ⋆(⋆(m, n), p) = ⋆(m, (⋆(n, p)). The way they are written in Definition 4.1.1.1 is called infix notation,. Given a function ⋆: A × B → C, we may write a ⋆ b rather than ⋆(a, b).

formal_items.title: Additive monoid of natural numbers
formal_items.text: Example 4.1.1.3 (Additive monoid of natural numbers). Let M = ℕ be the set of natural numbers. Let e = 0, and let ⋆: M × M → M denote addition, so that ⋆(4, 18) = 4 ⋆ 18 = 22. Then the equations m ⋆ 0 = m and 0 ⋆ m = m hold, and (m ⋆ n) ⋆ p = m ⋆ (n ⋆ p) because, as we learned in grade school, addition is associative. By assigning e and ⋆ in this way, we have given ℕ the structure of a monoid. We usually denote it (ℕ, 0, +).

formal_items.title: Monoids — Sometimes we are working with monoid
formal_items.text: Remark 4.1.1.4. Sometimes we are working with a monoid (M, e, ⋆), and the unit e and multiplication ⋆ are somehow clear from context. In this case we might refer to the set M as though it were the whole monoid. For example, if we were discussing the monoid from Example 4.1.1.3, we might refer to it as ℕ. The danger comes because sets may have multiple monoid structures (see Exercise 4.1.1.6).

formal_items.title: Monoids — Let be the set of natural
formal_items.text: Exercise 4.1.1.6. Let M = ℕ be the set of natural numbers. Taking e = 1 as the unit, devise a formula for ⋆ that gives ℕ the structure of a monoid.

formal_items.title: Monoids — Let denote the usual multiplication of
formal_items.text: Solution 4.1.1.6. Let ⋆ denote the usual multiplication of natural numbers, e.g., 5 ⋆ 7 = 35. Then for any m, n, p ∈ ℕ, we have 1 ⋆ m = m ⋆ 1 = m and (m ⋆ n) ⋆ p = m ⋆ (n ⋆ p), as required.

formal_items.title: Monoids — Find an operation on the set
formal_items.text: Exercise 4.1.1.7. Find an operation on the set M = {1, 2, 3, 4}, i.e., a legitimate function f : M × M → M, such that f cannot be the multiplication formula for a monoid on M. That is, either it is not associative or no element of M can serve as a unit.

formal_items.title: Monoids — In both Example 4.1.1.3 and Exercise
formal_items.text: Exercise 4.1.1.8. In both Example 4.1.1.3 and Exercise 4.1.1.6, the monoids (M, e, ⋆) satisfied an additional rule called commutativity, namely, m ⋆ n = n ⋆ m for every m, n ∈ M. There is a monoid (M, e, ⋆) in linear algebra that is not commutative; if you have background in linear algebra, what monoid (M, e, ⋆) might I be referring to?
